Nissan wants to build more of its new Rogue hybrid in the US. Small story, buried under the Trump-Xi headlines, but I keep coming back to it because of what it sits next to this month: Volkswagen cutting another 50,000 jobs and closing four plants, and a couple weeks before that, an actual industry pitch to boost EV range by bolting a gas engine back onto the car. Nobody in Detroit, Wolfsburg, or Yokohama is standing up to announce the EV transition is slowing down. That would be a policy statement, and policy statements get contradicted by the next election cycle. But watch where the capital actually goes, and a hybrid plant on US soil reads like a hedge running two directions at once: against tariffs, and against a consumer market that turned out to want gas range more than it wanted purity.

That's what I like about corporate strategy as a signal. It doesn't lie the way a press release does, because money committed to concrete is a bet, not a mood. This is the kind of adjustment industries make constantly, a thousand small decisions responding to real conditions while the official narrative lags a year behind. Nobody's wrong about the EV transition exactly. They're just renegotiating its timeline in the tooling budget instead of in a memo.

Markets, meanwhile, did their familiar Monday routine: oil down, yields down, stocks up, all of it leaning on hope that a Trump-Xi meeting produces something photogenic. I've stopped being surprised by how much of the tape now runs on one commodity's mood swings. I'd like a week where the story is something other than "oil eased, so we're fine."
